desc:
Some files in every codebase are avoided because nobody is sure what will break. Ecom Swift LLC offers code refactoring for faster development: we clean up the tangled parts of your app in small, tested steps without changing what users see.

## What is code refactoring?

Refactoring means restructuring existing code without changing its behavior. Functions become shorter, names become clearer, duplicated logic is merged and responsibilities are separated. From the outside, the app works exactly as before. On the inside, it becomes easier to read and change.

It is not a rewrite and it is not a feature. The point is to make the next feature cheaper, safer and quicker to build.

## Why messy code slows every project

Tangled code taxes every task. A developer who wants to change one rule must first read a thousand lines to find where it is applied, then guess what else depends on it. Estimates grow, bugs appear in unrelated places and new team members take longer to become useful.

The cost is hard to see because it is spread across everything. Nobody opens a ticket called "this module makes us slow". Teams simply feel it as a rising price for each change, until a request that should take a day takes a week.

## How refactoring pays back

The return comes in shorter build time and fewer regressions. When logic lives in one place, a change happens once. When names describe what code does, a reviewer can follow it without a guide. When tests surround a module, developers can change it without fear.

It also protects against knowledge loss. Code that only one person understands is a business risk. A cleaned module with a short note on its structure can be handed to someone new on their first week.

## What a safe refactor includes

- A choice of target based on where your team loses the most time.
- Tests written first around the current behavior, so we can prove nothing changed.
- Small steps, each one checked before the next begins.
- Clearer names for functions, variables, files and folders.
- Long functions split into pieces that each do one thing.
- Duplicate code merged into shared helpers.
- Dead code and unused files removed.
- Lint and formatting rules added so the clean state stays clean.
- Types added where they make the code safer to change.
- A before and after note on the structure, with a list of what to tackle next.

## How we work

We start by reading the code you flag, plus the places where your team feels the most friction. We agree on the modules in scope. Before touching them, we add tests that capture what they do today, including odd behavior you rely on. Then we restructure step by step, running the tests after each change.

The Basic package cleans one module under test cover and records the before and after. Standard covers several modules, removes duplicate and dead code, adds lint and format rules and sketches the new structure. Premium goes wider, with shared helpers, a folder structure, added types, more test coverage on the touched code, a coding guide for your team and a walkthrough call.

If we find a bug along the way, we tell you and fix it separately, so the refactor itself stays pure.

## What to do, and what to avoid

**Do:**
- Name the files your team dreads touching.
- Tell us which behavior must never change.
- Pause large feature work on the same files while we refactor.
- Review the merge requests in small pieces.
- Keep the new conventions after we leave.

**Avoid:**
- Refactoring and adding features in the same change.
- Cleaning code that has no tests and no plan to get them.
- Renaming everything at once.
- Expecting visible changes for users, because there should be none.
- Starting a full rewrite when a targeted clean-up would do.

## Who this is for

This suits a small team whose core module has grown too large to change safely. It suits a company preparing to hire developers who will need a readable codebase. It also suits a founder who wants to add features to code written quickly, without paying for a rewrite.

## What we need from you

Repository access as a collaborator or developer user, the list of modules or files that cause the most trouble and a way to run the project and its tests. We never need passwords. All changes arrive as reviewable merge requests in your own repository.
